best_for: Raspberry Pi owners setting up a board without a screen, who want Wi-Fi, SSH and a user account written onto the microSD card before first boot.
description:
Raspberry Pi Imager is the tool the makers of the Raspberry Pi boards recommend for putting an operating system on a microSD card or other boot drive. You run it on another computer, and it downloads the system image and writes it for you.

It walks you through tabs: device, OS, storage, then writing. The system Raspberry Pi suggests for your model sits at the top of the list. A setting called Exclude system drives, on by default, keeps you from wiping your computer's own disk by mistake. After writing, Imager checks the card, and the docs advise letting that finish. With no second computer, Network Install runs Imager on the Pi itself over a wired connection.

points.title: Card ready in one pass
points.text: Pick your Pi model, an operating system and the card, and Imager downloads and writes it. Raspberry Pi OS is the default, and other systems are on the list.

points.title: Set it up before it boots
points.text: You can set a hostname, user and password, time zone and keyboard, Wi-Fi including hidden networks, and SSH with a password or public key, and link Raspberry Pi Connect. A headless Pi then joins your network on its first start.

points.title: Telemetry is on by default
points.text: Imager reports which OS you chose, its own version, your computer's OS version, architecture and locale. Raspberry Pi keeps daily totals and raw logs for a week. You can switch it off in App Options.

points.title: Your own image list
points.text: Starting it with `--repo` and a URL points it at your own image repository, which helps when you set up many boards the same way.

points.title: Free and open source
points.text: Imager is free under the Apache 2.0 license, from Raspberry Pi Ltd.

points.title: Platforms differ here
points.text: The Windows listing keeps 26 versions but is at 2.0.8, with a 64-bit installer for all users. macOS (universal, macOS 13 or later) and the Linux Flatpak are at 2.0.12, current release only. The Flatpak carries Raspberry Pi's name, but Flathub does not mark it verified.
